lessons.title: Logic Gates, Boolean Algebra and Logic Families
lessons.overview: Digital systems represent information with two stable logic levels, 0 and 1. This unit builds the base for every later circuit: truth tables, basic and universal gates, Boolean laws, De Morgan’s theorems, and the practical differences between TTL and CMOS logic families.
objectives: Identify AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR gates from symbols and truth tables
Simplify small Boolean expressions using Boolean laws and De Morgan’s theorems
Explain why NAND and NOR are called universal gates
Compare TTL and CMOS using supply, power, speed, noise margin and fan-out
keyConcepts: AND gives 1 only when every input is 1; OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1; NOT complements a bit.
NAND = NOT(AND) and NOR = NOT(OR). Either gate alone can implement any Boolean function.
XOR is 1 when inputs are different; XNOR is 1 when inputs are equal.
Boolean identities such as A+0=A, A·1=A, A+A=A and A·A=A reduce circuit complexity.
De Morgan: (A·B)' = A' + B' and (A+B)' = A'·B'.
TTL uses bipolar transistors; CMOS uses complementary MOSFETs and generally offers lower static power.

diagrams.title: Universal-gate idea
diagrams.content:
NAND only:
NOT A = A NAND A
AND = (A NAND B) NAND (A NAND B)
OR  = (A NAND A) NAND (B NAND B)

NOR only:
NOT A = A NOR A
OR  = (A NOR B) NOR (A NOR B)
AND = (A NOR A) NOR (B NOR B)

lessons.theory:
## Digital logic
A digital circuit works with discrete voltage ranges interpreted as **logic 0** and **logic 1**. A gate is a small circuit that implements one Boolean operation. More complex blocks—adders, counters, registers and processors—are made by connecting gates.

## Boolean algebra
Boolean algebra uses variables that can be only 0 or 1. The most useful simplification laws are identity, null, idempotent, complement, absorption, distributive and De Morgan’s laws. Simplification matters because fewer gates normally mean lower cost, less delay and less power.

## Universal gates
NAND and NOR are universal because NOT, AND and OR can each be built using only NANDs or only NORs. In exams, show the algebra **and** the small gate construction.

## Logic families
A logic family defines the internal electronic technology and electrical compatibility of gates. Important parameters are propagation delay, power dissipation, fan-in, fan-out, noise margin and supply voltage. Never compare families using only one parameter; speed and power are often a trade-off.
commonMistakes: Treating XOR as OR; XOR becomes 0 for input 1,1.
Forgetting the bar over the entire expression when applying De Morgan’s theorem.
Calling NAND/NOR universal without showing how NOT, AND or OR can be formed.
Mixing ideal truth-table logic with real electrical parameters such as noise margin and fan-out.
examTips: Write the Boolean expression next to every truth table.
For De Morgan questions, complement every term and swap AND ↔ OR.
For TTL vs CMOS, use a comparison table with at least four parameters.
If asked for a universal-gate realization, draw each NAND/NOR stage clearly.

practiceQuestions.question: Which gate is 1 only when two inputs are different?
practiceQuestions.explanation: XOR implements inequality for two inputs.

practiceQuestions.question: Using De Morgan’s theorem, (A+B)' equals:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Complement of OR becomes AND of the complemented inputs.

practiceQuestions.question: Why is NAND called universal?
options: All basic Boolean functions can be built from NAND alone
practiceQuestions.explanation: NOT, AND and OR can all be synthesized using only NAND gates.

workedExamples.title: Simplify a Boolean expression
workedExamples.solution: Use absorption law: A + A·B = A.
workedExamples.explanation: When A=1 the output is already 1; when A=0 both terms are 0, so B cannot change the result.

lessons.revisionSummary: Know every basic gate truth table, the two De Morgan identities, the reason NAND/NOR are universal, and the meaning of propagation delay, power dissipation, noise margin and fan-out.
cheatSheet: De Morgan swaps AND and OR while complementing each variable
CMOS: very high input impedance and low static power

flashcards.back: Maximum number of standard logic inputs that one output can drive reliably.

flashcards.front: State De Morgan for an AND expression.

flashcards.back: Equality: it outputs 1 when the inputs are the same.

vivaQuestions.question: Why are NAND and NOR universal gates?
vivaQuestions.modelAnswer: Because NOT, AND and OR—and therefore any Boolean function—can be implemented using only NAND gates or only NOR gates.

vivaQuestions.question: Define propagation delay.
vivaQuestions.modelAnswer: The time between an input logic transition and the corresponding valid output transition.

lessons.title: Adders, Subtractors, Multiplexers, Encoders and Decoders
lessons.overview: A combinational circuit has no memory: its output depends only on the present input combination. This unit covers arithmetic circuits and the data-routing/code-conversion blocks most often used in digital systems.
objectives: Design half and full adders/subtractors
Explain MUX and DEMUX operation
Differentiate encoder and decoder
Use a comparator to determine equality or magnitude
keyConcepts: Half adder adds A and B: Sum=A⊕B, Carry=A·B.
Full adder adds A, B and Cin and can be built from two half adders plus an OR gate.
Multiplexer selects one of many data inputs using select lines; 2^n inputs require n select lines.
Demultiplexer routes one input to one of many outputs.
Decoder converts an n-bit code to up to 2^n active outputs; encoder performs the reverse function.
Magnitude comparator produces A>B, A=B and A<B outputs.

diagrams.title: Full adder using two half adders

lessons.theory:
## Combinational logic
There is no feedback memory element in an ideal combinational circuit. A systematic design method is: define inputs/outputs → create truth table → derive Boolean expressions → simplify → draw circuit → verify.

## Arithmetic blocks
A half adder cannot accept a carry from a previous stage, so multi-bit addition requires **full adders**. Cascading full adders creates a ripple-carry adder; the carry propagation creates delay.

## Data selection
A multiplexer is a digitally controlled switch. It is useful not only for routing data but also for implementing Boolean functions by wiring data inputs to 0, 1 or variables.

## Code conversion
Decoders are used for memory/device selection and display driving. Encoders reduce one-of-many inputs to a compact binary code; a priority encoder resolves the case where multiple inputs are active.
commonMistakes: Using half adder where Cin is required
Reversing encoder and decoder direction
Forgetting that 8:1 MUX needs 3 select lines
Writing MUX minterms with the wrong complemented select variable
examTips: Memorize half/full-adder expressions
For a 4:1 MUX, write selection table before Boolean equation
Draw clean block symbols with select and enable pins
State whether decoder outputs are active-high or active-low when relevant

practiceQuestions.question: How many select lines does an 8:1 MUX require?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 2^3=8, so three select bits identify one of eight inputs.

practiceQuestions.question: The full-adder Sum output is:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sum is odd parity of A, B and Cin.

practiceQuestions.question: A decoder generally converts:
options: n-bit code to up to 2^n outputs
Many data inputs to one output
practiceQuestions.explanation: An n-to-2^n decoder activates the output represented by its binary input.

workedExamples.title: Choose a MUX size
workedExamples.problem: You must select one of 16 sensor-status bits. How many select lines are needed?
workedExamples.solution: n=log2(16)=4 select lines; use a 16:1 multiplexer.
workedExamples.explanation: Four binary bits can represent 16 input indices.

lessons.revisionSummary: Combinational outputs depend only on current inputs. Master the full-adder equations and the direction/purpose of MUX, DEMUX, encoder, decoder and comparator.
cheatSheet: Decoder expands code; encoder compresses code

flashcards.back: Encoder converts active input to code; decoder converts code to one-of-many outputs.

vivaQuestions.question: What is the main limitation of a half adder?
vivaQuestions.modelAnswer: It has no carry-in input, so it cannot directly add a bit plus a carry from a lower stage.

lessons.title: Flip-Flops, Counters and Registers
lessons.overview: Sequential circuits contain memory, so their outputs depend on present inputs and previous state. Flip-flops store one bit; counters move through a state sequence; registers store or shift groups of bits.
objectives: Differentiate latch and flip-flop
Explain SR, JK, D and T flip-flops
Compare synchronous and asynchronous counters
Describe SISO, SIPO, PISO and PIPO registers
keyConcepts: A latch is level-sensitive; a flip-flop is normally edge-triggered.
SR stores/reset-set state but has a forbidden/invalid combination in the basic form.
JK removes the SR invalid case; J=K=1 toggles.
D flip-flop transfers D to Q on the active clock edge and is widely used in registers.
T flip-flop toggles when T=1 and is useful for counters.
Ripple counters clock each stage from the previous stage; synchronous counters share a common clock.
Shift registers move bits serially and/or expose them in parallel.
formulas: n flip-flops can represent up to 2^n states
For a divide-by-2 toggle stage: fout = fclk/2

tables.title: Flip-flop action summary
rows: Set, reset, hold; avoid invalid basic-SR state

diagrams.title: 4-bit ripple counter
diagrams.content:
CLK → [FF0] → [FF1] → [FF2] → [FF3]
       Q0      Q1      Q2      Q3
Each stage toggles from the previous stage, so delays accumulate.

diagrams.title: 4-bit SIPO register
diagrams.content:
Serial In → [DFF]→[DFF]→[DFF]→[DFF]
              Q0     Q1     Q2     Q3
                 common clock

lessons.theory:
## Memory and clocking
The key difference from combinational logic is **state**. A clock coordinates when state changes. Setup and hold requirements ensure the input is stable around the active clock edge.

## Flip-flops
The D flip-flop is easiest to reason about: on the active edge, the next Q becomes D. JK and T flip-flops are convenient for toggling/state-machine counters.

## Counters
In an asynchronous/ripple counter, the first flip-flop is clocked externally and later stages are clocked by earlier outputs. It is simple but propagation delays accumulate. A synchronous counter drives all flip-flops from one clock and uses combinational next-state logic, so it is faster and more predictable.

## Registers
Registers are groups of flip-flops. Shift registers perform serial/parallel conversion, delay sequences and temporary storage.
commonMistakes: Calling a ripple counter synchronous
Forgetting JK toggle when J=K=1
Confusing SIPO with PISO
Ignoring propagation delay in asynchronous counters
examTips: Draw clock connection clearly when comparing sync vs async counters
Use a state/count table for counter questions
For shift registers, expand SISO/SIPO/PISO/PIPO before explaining
Mention race-around in level-triggered JK and its remedies when asked

practiceQuestions.question: Which flip-flop has Q(next)=D?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The D flip-flop captures the D input on its active clock edge.

practiceQuestions.question: In a JK flip-flop, J=K=1 causes:
practiceQuestions.explanation: JK removes the SR invalid case by defining 1,1 as toggle.

practiceQuestions.question: Which counter clocks all stages together?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A synchronous counter applies the same clock to all flip-flops.

workedExamples.title: Counter capacity
workedExamples.problem: How many flip-flops are required for a mod-10 counter?
workedExamples.solution: Find n such that 2^n ≥ 10. 2^3=8 is insufficient, 2^4=16, so n=4.
workedExamples.explanation: Unused states are handled by reset/next-state logic.

lessons.revisionSummary: Sequential logic remembers state. D stores data, JK/T are good for toggle behavior, synchronous counters are faster than ripple counters, and shift registers perform serial/parallel conversion.

flashcards.back: Propagation delay accumulates from stage to stage.

vivaQuestions.question: Differentiate synchronous and asynchronous counters.
vivaQuestions.modelAnswer: A synchronous counter clocks all flip-flops from one common clock; an asynchronous/ripple counter clocks later stages from previous outputs, causing cumulative propagation delay.

lessons.title: 8051 Architecture, Memory and I/O Ports
lessons.overview: The classic 8051 is an 8-bit microcontroller that combines a CPU, internal RAM, I/O ports, timers, serial interface and interrupt control on one chip. Understanding its block diagram and special-function registers is essential before assembly programming or interfacing.
objectives: Identify major 8051 blocks
Explain CPU registers and PSW flags
Describe internal data-memory organization
Explain the four 8-bit I/O ports and alternate functions
keyConcepts: 8051 has an 8-bit ALU and accumulator A; B assists multiply/divide.
DPTR is a 16-bit data pointer formed by DPH and DPL; PC is the 16-bit program counter.
SP is the stack pointer; PSW contains status flags and register-bank selection bits.
Internal lower RAM includes register banks, a bit-addressable area and general-purpose RAM.
Special Function Registers (SFRs) control ports, timers, serial communication, interrupts and CPU state.
P0–P3 are four 8-bit ports; some pins have alternate bus, serial, interrupt and timer functions.

tables.title: Port alternate roles
rows: General I/O or multiplexed low address/data bus
General I/O or high address bus
I/O plus RxD, TxD, INT0/1, T0/1, RD, WR alternate functions

diagrams.title: Simplified 8051 block diagram
diagrams.content:
+------------------- 8051 -------------------+
| CPU/ALU  A B PSW  PC DPTR SP              |
|     |            internal bus              |
| ROM/Code   RAM/SFR   Timers   Serial UART  |
| Interrupt Control            Oscillator    |
| P0       P1       P2       P3              |
+--------------------------------------------+

codeExamples.title: Write alternating values to Port 1
codeExamples.explanation: Direct SFR addressing writes an 8-bit immediate pattern to the Port 1 latch.

lessons.theory:
## Microprocessor vs microcontroller
A microcontroller integrates the CPU and common peripherals needed for embedded control. The 8051’s on-chip ports, timers, serial interface and interrupt logic make it suitable for small control systems.

## CPU registers
The accumulator is central to arithmetic/logical instructions. The **PSW** holds Carry, Auxiliary Carry, Overflow, Parity and register-bank control bits. **DPTR** is important when accessing tables or external memory.

## Memory organization
The classic architecture separates program/code space conceptually from data space. Lower internal RAM supports register banks and bit-addressable storage; SFR addresses map control registers. Always distinguish an ordinary RAM byte from an SFR at a named address.

## Ports
Ports are not interchangeable in every hardware design because some pins carry alternate functions. P0 also differs electrically in the classic device when used as general I/O and may need external pull-ups.
commonMistakes: Calling DPTR an 8-bit register
Confusing PC with DPTR
Forgetting that P3 pins have alternate peripheral functions
Treating SFR area as ordinary general-purpose RAM
examTips: Draw the architecture as labelled blocks, not just a list
Mention A, B, PSW, PC, DPTR and SP when asked for CPU organization
For port questions, write P3 alternate functions
Use hexadecimal notation consistently

practiceQuestions.question: Which 8051 register is 16-bit and commonly points to data/table addresses?
practiceQuestions.explanation: DPTR consists of DPH and DPL and is a 16-bit pointer.

practiceQuestions.question: Which register contains CPU flags?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Program Status Word contains carry, auxiliary carry, overflow, parity and bank-select bits.

practiceQuestions.question: How many basic I/O port bits are provided by four 8-bit ports?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 4 × 8 = 32 I/O lines before considering alternate functions.

workedExamples.title: Identify a register
workedExamples.problem: A program must point to a 16-bit table address before MOVC/MOVX-style access. Which register is normally used?
workedExamples.explanation: DPTR is the processor’s dedicated 16-bit data pointer.

lessons.revisionSummary: Memorize the 8051 block diagram, A/B/PSW/PC/DPTR/SP roles, RAM/SFR distinction, four ports and the alternate functions of Port 3.

flashcards.back: Status flags and register-bank selection bits.
Four: P0, P1, P2 and P3.

vivaQuestions.question: What is an SFR?
vivaQuestions.modelAnswer: A Special Function Register is a memory-mapped control/status register used for CPU state or peripherals such as ports, timers, serial interface and interrupts.

lessons.title: 8051 Addressing Modes, Instructions and Assembly Programs
lessons.overview: Programming the 8051 requires two skills: choosing the correct addressing mode and selecting instructions from data-transfer, arithmetic, logical, bit and branch groups. Small assembly programs become much easier when data flow is planned first.
objectives: Recognize common addressing modes
Classify 8051 instructions by purpose
Write small loops, arithmetic and port-control programs
Use flags and conditional branches correctly
keyConcepts: Immediate addressing embeds a constant in the instruction, e.g. MOV A,#25H.
Register addressing uses R0–R7; direct addressing names an internal RAM/SFR address.
Register-indirect addressing uses @R0/@R1 for internal data, while DPTR supports broader pointer use.
Data-transfer instructions move bytes/bits without necessarily changing arithmetic flags.
Arithmetic includes ADD/ADDC, SUBB, INC/DEC, MUL AB and DIV AB.
Logical/bit instructions include ANL, ORL, XRL, CLR, CPL, SETB and rotates.
Branch/control uses SJMP/LJMP, conditional jumps, DJNZ, CJNE, CALL and RET.
formulas: ADDC includes the carry flag: A ← A + operand + C
SUBB includes borrow through Carry: A ← A - operand - C

tables.title: Instruction groups
rows: MOV, MOVX, MOVC, PUSH, POP, XCH
ADD, ADDC, SUBB, INC, DEC, MUL, DIV
ANL, ORL, XRL, CLR, CPL, RL/RR
SJMP, LJMP, JZ/JNZ, DJNZ, CJNE, CALL, RET
SETB, CLR bit, CPL bit, JB/JNB

diagrams.title: Assembly-program workflow
diagrams.content: Define I/O/data → choose registers/addresses → initialize → loop/body → test flags/counters → branch → repeat/finish

codeExamples.title: Add ten bytes conceptually
codeExamples.code:
MOV R0,#30H     ; source start
MOV R2,#0AH     ; count = 10
CLR A
LOOP: ADD A,@R0
      INC R0
      DJNZ R2,LOOP
MOV 40H,A       ; store low-byte sum
codeExamples.explanation: R0 points to internal RAM, R2 is the loop counter, and DJNZ combines decrement with branch. A accumulates the low-byte result.

codeExamples.title: Toggle all Port 1 bits
codeExamples.code:
MOV P1,#00H
AGAIN: CPL P1
       ACALL DELAY
       SJMP AGAIN
codeExamples.explanation: CPL complements the port latch. A practical DELAY subroutine determines visible toggle rate.

lessons.theory:
## Addressing modes
Addressing mode answers: **where does the operand come from?** Immediate is a constant, register uses Rn, direct identifies an address/SFR, indirect obtains an address through a register, and indexed addressing is useful for code-memory tables.

## Instruction selection
Write the desired state change in plain language first. For example, ‘decrement count and repeat while non-zero’ maps naturally to **DJNZ**. ‘Compare two bytes and jump if not equal’ maps to **CJNE**.

## Flags
Carry matters for multi-byte arithmetic. ADDC propagates carry from a lower byte; SUBB incorporates borrow. Overflow is a signed-arithmetic signal and must not be confused with Carry.

## Program structure
Embedded assembly usually has an initialization section followed by an infinite control loop and optional subroutines/interrupt service routines. Preserve registers when a subroutine/ISR could destroy values the caller still needs.
commonMistakes: Omitting # for an immediate constant
Confusing direct address 30H with immediate #30H
Using ADD when multi-byte addition needs ADDC on higher bytes
Creating a loop without initializing its counter
examTips: State the addressing mode beside example instructions
Comment assembly lines so the examiner can follow data flow
For multi-byte arithmetic, explicitly show carry handling
Dry-run loops in a small register/memory table

practiceQuestions.question: MOV A,#30H uses which addressing mode?
Which instruction is convenient for a counted loop?
practiceQuestions.explanation: DJNZ decrements an operand and jumps while it remains non-zero.

practiceQuestions.question: Which instruction adds an operand plus the Carry flag?
practiceQuestions.explanation: ADDC is used to propagate carry in multi-byte addition.

workedExamples.title: 16-bit addition strategy
workedExamples.problem: Add low and high bytes of two 16-bit values.
workedExamples.solution: Clear C; ADD the low bytes and store result; load a high byte and use ADDC with the other high byte; store high result.
workedExamples.explanation: The Carry from low-byte addition must enter the high-byte calculation.

lessons.revisionSummary: Learn addressing modes by syntax, then memorize instruction families. # means immediate, @ means indirect, DJNZ is ideal for loops, and ADDC/SUBB are essential when Carry/borrow must propagate.
cheatSheet: CJNE compares and jumps if not equal

flashcards.back: Decrements its operand and jumps if the result is not zero.

flashcards.front: Why use ADDC on high bytes?
flashcards.back: To include Carry produced by the lower-byte addition.

vivaQuestions.question: Differentiate MOV A,30H and MOV A,#30H.
vivaQuestions.modelAnswer: MOV A,30H loads A from direct address 30H. MOV A,#30H loads the literal value 30H.

lessons.title: 8051 Interrupts, Timers and Peripheral Interfacing
lessons.overview: Interrupts let the 8051 respond to events without continuously polling. Interfacing connects the controller to real devices such as LEDs, switches, displays and converters. Good designs combine correct SFR configuration with safe electrical connections.
objectives: Explain interrupt sources and vectors
Describe interrupt enable/priority concepts
Use timers for delays/counting
Explain typical LED, switch, display and ADC/DAC interfacing
keyConcepts: Classic 8051 interrupt sources include external INT0, Timer0, external INT1, Timer1 and the serial port.
An interrupt vector is the fixed code address to which the CPU branches when an accepted interrupt occurs.
IE enables global/individual interrupts; IP controls basic priority selection.
Timers can count internal machine-cycle ticks or external events depending on configuration.
Interfacing requires correct voltage/current levels; a GPIO pin must not directly drive loads beyond its rating.
Switches often need pull resistors and debouncing; displays may need current-limiting resistors or driver ICs.
formulas: Timer overflow interval = counts × timer tick period
For an n-bit timer, full-range counts = 2^n

diagrams.title: Interrupt flow
diagrams.content: Main program → event occurs → finish current instruction → save return address → jump to vector/ISR → service event → RETI → resume main program

diagrams.title: Safe high-current load interface
diagrams.content:
8051 pin → resistor → transistor/driver → relay/load
                              ↑
                       flyback diode for coils
Never drive a relay coil directly from a GPIO pin.

codeExamples.title: External interrupt structure (concept)
codeExamples.code:
ORG 0000H
LJMP START
ORG 0003H       ; INT0 vector
LJMP INT0_ISR

START:
  SETB EA       ; global enable
  SETB EX0      ; enable INT0
MAIN: SJMP MAIN

INT0_ISR:
  CPL P1.0      ; example action
  RETI
codeExamples.explanation: The vector jumps to a dedicated ISR. RETI returns from interrupt and signals completion to the interrupt system.

lessons.theory:
## Why interrupts
Polling repeatedly asks a device whether an event occurred, consuming CPU time. Interrupts allow normal code to run until hardware requests attention. The CPU completes the current instruction, saves the return location, branches to the vector and runs an **ISR**.

## ISR rules
Keep an ISR short. Save/restore registers if the ISR modifies values used by the main program. Clear/acknowledge the event when required, and return with **RETI**, not ordinary RET.

## Timers
Timer configuration selects operating mode and whether the source is the internal clock path or an external pin. To create a delay, calculate required counts, preload the timer if necessary, start it, then detect overflow by polling or interrupt.

## Hardware interfacing
Digital logic correctness is not enough: check current, voltage, pull-ups, grounding and protection. Inductive loads need a driver and flyback diode. Mechanical switches bounce and may require hardware or software debounce.
commonMistakes: Using RET instead of RETI at the end of an ISR
Enabling an individual interrupt but forgetting global EA
Driving relay/motor loads directly from a port pin
Ignoring switch bounce
Using timer reload values without checking clock/tick assumptions
examTips: Draw interrupt flow plus vector table
Mention EA when explaining interrupt enable
For timer numericals, state the assumed oscillator/timer tick before calculating
In interfacing diagrams include driver/current-limiting components, not only signal wires

practiceQuestions.question: Which instruction should normally end an 8051 interrupt service routine?
practiceQuestions.explanation: RETI returns and informs the interrupt controller that interrupt servicing is complete.

practiceQuestions.question: Which bit/function enables interrupts globally?
practiceQuestions.explanation: EA is the global interrupt enable control.

practiceQuestions.question: Why should a relay coil not be driven directly from a GPIO pin?
options: It may require excessive current and generates inductive kickback
practiceQuestions.explanation: A transistor/driver and flyback protection are normally required.

workedExamples.title: Timer-delay planning
workedExamples.problem: A timer tick is 1 µs and a delay of 10 ms is needed. How many counts are required?
workedExamples.explanation: Then choose a timer mode and preload value compatible with its count range.

lessons.revisionSummary: Interrupts replace constant polling for important events. Know the five classic sources/vectors, EA/IE/IP concepts, RETI, timer-count logic, and safe electrical interfacing practices.

flashcards.back: Mechanical contacts can create multiple rapid transitions for one press.

vivaQuestions.question: Polling vs interrupt?
vivaQuestions.modelAnswer: Polling repeatedly checks status in software; an interrupt asynchronously requests CPU service only when an event occurs, allowing useful work between events.

revisionNotes: Digital Techniques & Microcontroller: begin with gates/Boolean algebra, then combinational blocks, sequential memory, 8051 architecture, assembly addressing/instructions, and finally interrupts/interfacing. The exam-friendly sequence is truth table → equation → circuit for digital logic, and block/register → instruction → program flow for 8051.

vivaBank.question: Why is a NAND gate universal?
vivaBank.modelAnswer: Any Boolean function can be constructed using only NAND gates because NAND can implement NOT, AND and OR.

vivaBank.question: Why is a synchronous counter faster than a ripple counter?
vivaBank.modelAnswer: All flip-flops receive the same clock, so clock-to-clock ripple propagation through each stage is avoided.

vivaBank.question: What is DPTR?
vivaBank.modelAnswer: A 16-bit Data Pointer register (DPH:DPL) used for table/external data addressing.
